data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

How can fossils, rock ages and seafloor patterns reveal moving continents? Compare several kinds of evidence and ask what each can establish.

1. Read **Following the Evidence** and watch how EVIDENCE piles up.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble** and the **Matching** game.
3. Follow **How We Figured It Out** — the timeline of the argument.
4. Sort the evidence in **What Kind of Boundary?**
5. Take the quiz — two questions ask what counts as EVIDENCE, not just what happened.
6. Fill in the **Cornell Notes** in your own words.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Earth Puzzle** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Explore: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.
9. Keep the **Three Ways Plates Meet** chart open while you sort — the three boundary types are the whole sort.

Use rocks and patterns to compare explanations. New evidence can change scientific understanding. 🌍

Picture panels: Plate material and spreading; Collision and subduction; Sliding and evidence; Landforms and deep rock. Text-free illustrations use editable captions and image-specific descriptions. Diagrams simplify scale, anatomy and processes; colors and tokens are explained in captions. Follow the lesson text for scientific context. Educator review is pending.

history.title: Following the Evidence
history.data:
## Following the Evidence

In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed that continents had once been joined and later moved apart. He assembled several kinds of evidence. Some scientists supported continental drift; many objected, especially to his proposed forces and the idea of continents pushing through oceanic rock.

The Atlantic margins of South America and Africa have complementary shapes. Their submerged continental margins fit better than modern shorelines, which erosion and sea-level change can alter. Related fossils, matching rock sequences and mountain belts also occur across the Atlantic. The distribution of Mesosaurus, an aquatic reptile, was more readily explained by connected land than by crossing a wide ocean. Antarctic coal records former vegetation and very different environmental conditions. Coal alone does not prove continental movement; climate can change too. The strength is in several independent lines of evidence agreeing.

New ocean-floor evidence helped transform the debate in the mid-twentieth century. Mapping revealed ridge systems in detail. Oceanic rocks tend to get older away from spreading ridges, and bands recording past magnetic polarity often mirror one another on opposite sides. Together with earthquake patterns and other measurements, these findings supported seafloor spreading and the broader theory of plate tectonics.

A tectonic plate is a slab of lithosphere: crust plus rigid uppermost mantle. Plates can carry both continents and ocean floor. They move over warmer, mostly solid mantle that deforms slowly over long times. They do not float on a global ocean of liquid magma. Gravity acting on sinking slabs and elevated lithosphere, together with mantle motion, contributes to plate movement; the balance varies.

At divergent boundaries, plates move apart. Along ocean ridges, rising mantle partly melts and magma forms new oceanic crust. Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the East African Rift shows continental extension.

At convergent boundaries, plates move toward one another. Dense oceanic lithosphere can descend beneath another plate at a subduction zone, producing a trench and often a volcanic belt. The Andes are an example. Where continental lithosphere collides, crust can shorten and thicken, helping build mountains such as the Himalayas.

At transform boundaries, plates slide past. Locked fault patches store elastic stress and may suddenly slip, producing earthquakes. Other patches creep. Earthquakes also occur at other boundaries and within plates.

Rates vary, but a few centimeters per year is common. Small annual movements become large changes over millions of years. Wegener died in 1930, decades before plate tectonics became widely accepted in the 1960s. His proposal was an important precursor, not the complete modern theory. Science can recognize strong evidence before every mechanism is known; new tests help distinguish competing explanations.

cards.target: The three boundary types and one example of each
essentialFacts: Divergent: plates pull apart, magma rises, new crust forms (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland).
Convergent: plates push together, one dives under or both crumple upward (the Himalayas).

history.title: How We Figured It Out

data.progressionLabel: TIMELINE: A noticed coincidence (1596) → Accepted theory (1960s)

items.event: Mapmaker Abraham Ortelius notices that the Atlantic coastlines look like they could fit together.
Alfred Wegener proposes continental drift, using matching coastlines, fossils, rock layers, and climate clues.
Many scientists reject Wegener’s proposed mechanism, while some support continental drift.
Wegener dies during a Greenland expedition; continental drift remains disputed.
Postwar ocean mapping reveals ridge and trench systems in increasing detail.
Harry Hess proposes sea-floor spreading: new crust forms at ridges and spreads outward.
Magnetic stripes on the sea floor are found to mirror each other on both sides of the ridge — powerful confirming evidence.
Plate tectonics is assembled from these pieces and becomes the unifying theory of modern geology.

questions.question: What was a major reason many geologists rejected Wegener’s drift model?
options: His fossil evidence turned out to be faked
The coastlines do not actually fit together
He could not explain what force would move the continents
He was not a trained scientist
questions.correctAnswer: He could not explain what force would move the continents

questions.question: Identical Mesosaurus fossils appear in South America and Africa. Why is that strong evidence?
options: Fossils are always found on exactly one continent
Mesosaurus was a strong ocean swimmer
The fossils are the same age as the Atlantic Ocean
Their distribution is more readily explained by a former connection than a wide-ocean crossing
questions.correctAnswer: Their distribution is more readily explained by a former connection than a wide-ocean crossing

questions.question: The Himalayas are still growing today. What kind of boundary explains that?
options: Convergent — India is pushing into Asia and both crumple upward
Divergent — the plates are pulling apart and magma fills the gap
Transform — the plates are sliding sideways past each other
None — mountains form only from volcanoes
questions.correctAnswer: Convergent — India is pushing into Asia and both crumple upward

questions.question: Which later discovery helped explain how ocean floor and continents could move as parts of plates?
options: Better maps of the continents' coastlines drawn from satellite photographs
Sea-floor spreading discovered by mapping the ocean bottom
Finding more matching fossils on land on both sides of the Atlantic
Measuring the temperature of Earth's core with deep drilling
questions.correctAnswer: Sea-floor spreading discovered by mapping the ocean bottom

questions.question: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
options: Several meters every single day, fast enough to feel
Only in sudden jumps during earthquakes, staying still between them
Around one full kilometer every year
A few centimeters a year — about as fast as fingernails grow
questions.correctAnswer: A few centimeters a year — about as fast as fingernails grow

questions.question: Antarctic coal records former vegetation. What does this support, and why is coal alone not enough to prove continental drift?
questions.expectedAnswer: Coal supports past vegetation and environmental conditions different from today. Climate can change without plate motion, so coal alone does not prove drift. Combine it with independent fossil, rock and seafloor evidence.

questions.question: How did later evidence strengthen and change Wegener’s proposal? Can evidence matter before a mechanism is fully understood?
questions.expectedAnswer: Seafloor ages, magnetic bands and earthquake patterns supported spreading, subduction and moving lithospheric plates. This differed from continents plowing through ocean floor. Strong evidence can matter before a mechanism is fully known; scientists still compare alternatives and test explanations.

reflections.text: Which piece of Wegener's evidence would have convinced you? Why that one?
Name something people believe today that you think might be overturned by future evidence.

data.question: Will the continents crash back together someday? 🌎
data.answer: Another supercontinent may form over hundreds of millions of years. Several scenarios are modeled, but its shape, timing and location are uncertain.

data.question: What plate am I on right now?
data.answer: Most of North America sits on the North American Plate, which reaches far into the Atlantic. Parts of coastal California sit on the Pacific Plate instead. That is why the two grind past each other along the San Andreas.

data.question: Can we predict earthquakes yet?
data.answer: Not the way people want. Scientists can say which areas are at risk. They can say roughly how often big quakes happen. They cannot say the day or the hour. Anyone claiming exact prediction is overselling.

data.question: Is Mount Everest still growing? 🏔️
data.answer: Yes, by a few millimeters a year, as India keeps pressing north. Erosion and earthquakes shave some of that back off.

data.question: What is the Ring of Fire?
data.answer: The Pacific margin has many volcanoes and earthquake zones. Subduction accounts for many volcanic belts, but not every boundary around the Pacific is convergent.

data.question: Was Pangaea the only supercontinent?
data.answer: No. It is just the most recent, and the best documented. Geologists have evidence for earlier ones, like Rodinia. The continents have come together and broken apart several times.

data.title: Reading a Coastline Like Wegener
data.instructions: Build an evidence-based case for a former continental connection, then compare it with seafloor ages and the plate-motion model. Mark observations, interpretations and uncertainty separately.
data.fitReason: The lesson is about how evidence and mechanism together make a scientific case. An exploration lets students assemble both halves for a real pair of coasts.

brief.context: Your class has maps of plate boundaries, fossils, rocks and ocean-floor ages. At spreading ridges the youngest crust is near the axis and ages generally increase outward; subduction recycles older oceanic lithosphere.
brief.audience: A skeptical panel of classmates playing the 1920s geologists
brief.drivingQuestion: For one pair of coastlines that look like they fit, what evidence shows they were once joined, and what does the ocean floor between them have to look like if that is true?
brief.seedDirection: Start with margin shapes, then test the proposed connection against independent fossil, rock and seafloor evidence.
lockedLessonFacts: Wegener's evidence: matching coastlines, identical fossils, matching rock layers, and climate clues such as coal under Antarctic ice.
Many scientists rejected Wegener’s proposed forces; later seafloor and earthquake evidence supported the broader plate model.
At divergent boundaries, magma rises at a ridge and makes new crust that spreads outward.
Magnetic stripes in sea-floor rock mirror each other on both sides of the ridge.
Continents ride on plates; they do not plow through the ocean floor.
openQuestions: Where is the ridge between your two coasts, and is the youngest sea floor along it?
Do the rock types on each coast actually match, or only the shapes?
If the coasts have been moving apart for millions of years, how far apart should they be now at a few centimeters per year?
stakeholders: Future students who will use your case as a model
The scientists whose evidence you are reusing
criteria: The case uses at least three different kinds of evidence, not only coastline shape
It names the mechanism and points to a feature on the ocean-floor map that shows it
Each piece of evidence is labeled as strong, supportive, or weak
Uses at least four glossary words correctly
constraints: Only maps and data your class actually has
The panel may ask 'how do you know?' about any claim, so every claim needs a source line
Two pages including the annotated map
brief.deliverable: An annotated map of your two coastlines with the evidence marked on it, plus a one-page written case that ends with the mechanism: what the sea floor between the coasts must be doing.

parallelExample.context: A student noticed that the Red Sea looks like a crack opening between Africa and Arabia.
parallelExample.move: A student compares Red Sea margin shapes with published ridge, seafloor-age and plate-motion data. She records sources and uncertainty, then checks whether the data support opening between Africa and Arabia.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: An explanation should agree with several observations. A ridge pattern supports spreading but does not by itself reveal every force moving the plates.

supports.frameStarter: These coasts were once joined because ____, ____, and ____. The mechanism is ____, which we can see in ____.
frameChoices: Match the coastline shapes and check rock types on each side
Trace a fossil found on both coasts and ask whether it could have crossed an ocean
Find the ridge and the youngest sea floor between the coasts
Estimate how long the separation took at a few centimeters per year
coachPrompts: Which of your evidence types would Wegener have had, and which one only arrived after 1947?
If the panel says 'coincidence,' which evidence answers them?
Does your mechanism explain the direction the coasts moved?

data.coachHint: Wegener had the what. Your case needs the how. Find the ridge.
data.sourceExcerpt: Along that ridge, new rock was erupting and pushing outward. Even better, magnetic stripes frozen into that rock matched in mirror image on both sides. The sea floor was spreading.
